title: Integrated targeted and non-targeted analysis of water sample extracts with micro-scale UHPLC–MS
author: Deyerling, Schramm

steps.title: Remove water and spike cartridges
steps.instruction: Remove excess water from each XAD sampling cartridge by passing a gentle stream of nitrogen for 5 min, then spike the still‑wet polymeric resin with the internal‑standard mixture containing all target analytes as mass‑labeled compounds.

steps.title: Soxhlet extraction of cartridges
steps.instruction: Transfer the spiked cartridges to a Soxhlet apparatus and extract with 800 mL acetone for 16 h (≈60 extraction cycles). The following day, evaporate the extract by rotary evaporation to ~200 mL, pass the concentrate through glass filters packed with dry sodium sulfate to remove residual water, and finally evaporate to a final volume of ~2 mL, ready for solid‑phase extraction.

steps.title: Dialyze virtual organisms
steps.instruction: Place each virtual organism (VO) in a 250 mL Erlenmeyer flask containing 100 mL acetonitrile:methanol (50:50, v/v). Gently shake on an orbital shaker for 16 h overnight. After dialysis, remove the VO, spike the dialysate with the mass‑labeled standards, and evaporate to ~2 mL, ready for SPE cleanup.

steps.title: Condition SPE cartridge
steps.instruction: On a vacuum manifold, condition each SPE cartridge sequentially with 5 mL acetonitrile:methanol (50:50, v/v) followed by 5 mL ultrapure water.

steps.title: Load sample onto SPE
steps.instruction: Transfer the prepared extract to the conditioned SPE cartridge. Rinse the original sample flask three times with ~0.2 mL ultrapure water. For direct SPE of water samples, pass 250 mL water (spiked with mass‑labeled standards) through the cartridge at a flow rate of 4 mL min⁻¹.

steps.title: Wash, dry, and elute SPE
steps.instruction: Wash the cartridge with 5 mL ultrapure water, then dry under gentle vacuum for about 40 min. Elute the retained analytes with two portions of 5 mL acetonitrile:methanol (50:50, v/v) (total 10 mL) into a pear‑shaped flask.

steps.title: Evaporate eluate and adjust volume
steps.instruction: Rotary‑evaporate the eluate to ~200 µL, transfer it to a 1.5 mL polypropylene tube while rinsing the flask three times with acetonitrile:methanol (50:50, v/v). Finally, bring the sample to a total volume of ~200 µL by evaporating excess solvent under a gentle nitrogen stream while heating to 40 °C.

steps.title: Set MS parameters for non‑target run
steps.instruction: Inject the prepared sample after the targeted analysis. Set the mass spectrometer cone voltage to 25 V and the collision energy to 5 V to minimise fragmentation. Run a blank injection immediately before each sample to allow background subtraction.

steps.title: Calculate retention time index (RTI)
steps.instruction: Use the signals of the mass‑labeled internal standards to calibrate the chromatographic system on a retention‑time index scale ranging from 50 (first eluting compound) to 150 (last eluting compound). Compute each RTI_i with the equation: RTI_i = (log P_i – log P_{i‑1})·(150‑50)/(log P_max – log P_min) + RTI_{i‑1}. Here log P_max and log P_min are the partition‑coefficient values of the most and least retained standards, respectively.

steps.title: Convert RTI to log P
steps.instruction: For each unknown suspect, obtain its RTI by linear interpolation between the two nearest standards, then convert that RTI back to a log P value using the linear correlation established from the calibrated standards.

steps.title: Non‑target data processing workflow
steps.instruction: Process each sample through the following steps: 1) Subtract the blank‑injection signal (MassLynx 4.1). 2) Convert the blank‑corrected data to NetCDF format with DataBridge‑tool for MZmine 2.14 processing. 3) Crop irrelevant chromatogram regions (early elution and re‑equilibration). 4) Generate a peak list from the total ion chromatogram, keeping peaks with a minimum height of 50 counts s⁻¹. 5) Deconvolute overlapping peaks into separate rows. 6) Apply an isotopic‑pattern filter to remove duplicate isotope peaks. 7) Visually inspect the suspect list and discard obvious noise. 8) Calculate the partition coefficient for each remaining suspect using its retention time (RTI). 9) Identify suspects by searching STOFF‑IDENT, DAIOS, and MassBank with exact mass, calculated log P, and observed fragment ions.

description: The analysis of organic trace compounds in water is a challenging task requiring analyte enrichment in most analytical approaches. For the analysis of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) we routinely applied passive samplers to which we refer to as virtual organisms [1], [2], [3]. In a more recent study, passive sampling was accompanied by the active on-site enrichment of PAHs on self-packed glass cartridges with polymeric resin [4]. This active sampling technique allowed us to cover a wider range of more polar analytes by the variation of the employed polymeric resin. Therefore, we developed a new instrumental approach allowing the analysis of samples from different sample origin toward a more polar group of analytes like pharmaceutical residues and polar herbicides. Method development for some selected target compounds as well as for non-target analysis was carried out on a nano-scale UHPLC–MS system coupled to a Q-TOF mass spectrometer. The nano-scale chromatography system, commonly applied in proteomic approaches, promises detection with high sensitivity and less matrix suppression which are abilities of which also environmental analysis could benefit. With operating the chromatography system with a micro-scale analytical column, we could further enlarge the application spectrum of this universal instrument.
